newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan urges action on long-term budget deficit.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan urges action on long-term budget deficit.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan said Wednesday lawmakers should not lose sight of long-term budget deficit problems associated with the baby-boom generation retiring.

Greenspan told the Senate Banking Committee that he supported current efforts to balance the budget in the short-run. He asked lawmakers to be mindful of the "shock" to the fiscal system after 2010 when baby-boomers reach retirement.
Greenspan told the committee that merely getting a balanced budget by 2002, as called for in the current budget package, is not enough.
"It is important to recognize that after 2002 the deficit starts to drift up again and becomes a significant problem as you move into the second decade of the 21st century," Greenspan said.
He urged lawmakers not to wait too long to deal with the long-term budget problem because of the need for people to prepare for any changes in Social Security and other retirment laws.
Greenspan said the country would reap great economic benefits, including lower long-term interest rates, from addressing the long-term budget deficit problems.
He noted that while long-term interest rates have declined in recent years, they were still above levels seen in the 1950's and 1960's.

Greenspan said that was due to the so-called "inflation" premium in rates because of investor concerns about government spending and budget deficits. He said there was an ability to lower the inflation premium and the economy would benefit greatly by the added investment and economic growth that lower inflation and interest rates would bring.

"It is a process we should endeavor to foster and the major way of doing it is to recognize that passing the zero budget deficit line doesn't mean you should stop there," Greenspan told lawmakers. "There is nothing that says that." "On the
contrary the benefits that are achieved from going from high budget deficits, to low budget deficits, to balance, continue as you move over that line into surpluses," he added.
"I would think that understanding the process and fostering that process would be something of considerable value to the country," Greenspan said.
His comments were in answer to a question from the panel on whether any surplus money should be used to pay down the national debt or other purposes.
